transcript.text: Bosch induction hob PUE611BB1E making a loud buzzing/humming noise when I put my big stockpot on high. Is it about to break?

Almost certainly not. Buzzing or humming on high power is one of the most common induction hob complaints, and Bosch's own manual lists it as normal operating noise rather than a fault.

## Why it happens

Induction works by creating a rapidly alternating magnetic field that makes the pan itself heat up. At high settings, especially PowerBoost, that field is strong enough to make parts of the pan vibrate slightly, which you hear as a hum or buzz. It's usually worse with:

• Multi-layer (clad) pans, like steel with an aluminium or copper core. The layers can vibrate against each other. Big stockpots are very often built this way.
• Large, heavy pots, which need the zone running hard for a long time.
• Pans with a separate base disc bonded onto the bottom.
• Pans that are nearly empty or dry. Noise often drops once there's water or food in them.
• A pot bigger than the zone, so the magnetic field isn't evenly covered.

You may also hear:
• A fan running underneath to cool the electronics. It can keep going for a few minutes after you switch off.
• A clicking or ticking, especially at lower or medium settings, as the hob cycles power on and off.
• A whistling or high-pitched whine with some cookware or when using two zones on the same side together.

## Quick things to try

1. Turn it down a notch or two. Going from boost to 8 or 9 often cuts the noise dramatically while barely slowing things down.
2. Use the right-sized zone. Put the stockpot on the largest zone and centre it.
3. Make sure the pot has contents before cranking it up.
4. Try a different pan on the same zone. If the noise disappears, it's the pot, not the hob.

## When it would be worth worrying

Get it looked at (Bosch service, or check your warranty) if you notice:

• Noise with every pan, even at low settings
• A burning smell, crackling, or sparking
• Error codes (e.g. "E" or "F" codes) or zones cutting out unexpectedly
• The fan not running and the hob overheating or shutting down
• Grinding or rattling that sounds mechanical, which could be a failing fan
• Any cracks in the glass. Stop using it immediately if so.

If it's just loud with that one big pot on high and otherwise works perfectly, it's the pot and the physics, not a sign of an impending breakdown.

Thanks, that's reassuring. I did try a different pan: my heavy cast iron pot is quiet on the same zone, but the new stockpot and a cheap frying pan both buzz. It's also much quieter at 6 and below. So it sounds like it's the pans rather than the hob?

Yes, that's a textbook result pointing to the pans, not the hob.

Why your test is so conclusive:

• Cast iron is quiet because it's one solid, heavy piece of metal. There are no layers or bonded discs to vibrate against each other, and the sheer mass dampens any vibration.
• The stockpot and cheap frying pan buzz most likely because they're multi-layer or have a disc bonded to the base. Cheaper pans also tend to be thinner, which makes them vibrate more easily.
• Quieter at 6 and below fits perfectly: less power means a weaker magnetic field and less vibration. A failing hob component would typically make noise regardless of the pan.

What you can do:

• Live with it. It's harmless to both the hob and the pans. Many people just get used to it.
• Bring things to the boil on high, then drop to 6 or so to simmer. A stockpot rarely needs full power once it's going.
• Fill the pot before heating rather than heating it empty.
• When replacing pans, look for heavier, fully clad construction or cast iron/enamelled cast iron. Reviews often mention whether a pan is noisy on induction.

Also, my last message got cut off. The final point was that grinding or rattling from inside the hob itself (rather than from the pan) can indicate a failing cooling fan and would be worth getting checked. But nothing you've described suggests that.
